messages.author: bcfb6bc9f75aae0f
messages.subject: Problem with a simple mixture of normals.
parts:
Dear list,

I am trying to attack the problem studied by Carlin & Chib (1995) in the first part of their paper. This has given the "Pines" example in vol III of BUGS examples. It is a simple linear regression problem of a dependent variable Y on either X or Z, closely related continuous variables. In order to compare the merits of those fits, Carlin & Chib introduce a "state" variable stating at each iteration of the sampler which of the models will be used. The posterior distribution of pi gives an idea of the relative strength of the models (about the same meaning as the Bayes factor).

I'm trying to fit Y by a mixture of regression of X and Z.

A first model (M1.stan) just fits these two models, with no difficulty whatsoever. However, I find myself unable to fit to a mixture (M2.stant ; I followed the mixture example of the Stan user's guide), and am unable to understand why. I get tons of "Metropolis rejection" messages and get four chains with no movement at all, except when I try to specify 'init="random", which quickly gives me :
"Initialization failed after 100 attempts.  Try specifying initial values, reducing ranges of constrained values, or reparameterizing the model."

Replacing "log_sum_exp(lp1+log(pi), lp2+log(1.0-pi))" by the equivalent but numerically unstable "log(pi*exp(lp1)+(1.0-pi)*exp(lp2))" quickly converges ... to nonsensical values !

I am at the end of my rope here... Can someone suggest something ? I think I'm missing an important point.

messages.author: d4fb714af6c90658
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Problem with a simple mixture of normals.
parts:
I think that your model could be improved. However, I'd start by replacing:

lp__<-lp__+log_sum_exp(log(pi)+lp1, log((1.0-pi)+lp2));

with:

lp__<-lp__+log_sum_exp(log(pi)+lp1, log(1.0-pi)+lp2);

HTH

Sergio

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Problem with a simple mixture of normals.
parts:
Other than the typo, the way you're coding mixtures looks
OK to me.

There's always a problem with mixtures in that they can wander
off into very low variance solutions. (Where one mixture component
accounts for one data point with zero variance.)

What happens if you tighten up the priors around the parameters
to near where you want them to be?

When you say the distribution of pi is flat, you mean pi = 0.5?

- Bob

P.S. You don't need the truncations on truncations with constant
parameters.

s~cauchy(0, 5) T[0,];
t~cauchy(0, 5) T[0,];

You also don't need the uniform on pi.

P.P.S. For arithmetic stability and speed, there's also a
log1m(u) == log(1 - u) function, that you can use
in place of log(1 - pi).

Other than the typo, the way you're coding mixtures looks
OK to me.

There's always a problem with mixtures in that they can wander
off into very low variance solutions.  (Where one mixture component
accounts for one data point with zero variance.)
Doesn't seem to be the case here.

What happens if you tighten up the priors around the parameters
to near where you want them to be?
Ditto,with slightly lesser variances. Traces show that chains converge on *different* central values for the variance parameters.
When you say the distribution of pi is flat, you mean pi = 0.5?
No, I mean almost uniform(0,1)

P.S.  You don't need the truncations on truncations with constant
parameters.

Reminds myelf that s and t are variance parameters... Is there a computational cost for this truncation ?
You also don't need the uniform on pi.
More of a placeholder for a future dirichlet prior on more than two models.

P.P.S.  For arithmetic stability and speed, there's also a
         log1m(u) == log(1 - u) function, that you can use
         in place of log(1 - pi).

Thank you. I didn't know that. 

- Emmanuel

Short answer: yes, but it shouldn't be too bad if there
aren't that many calls.

Longer answer: We haven't linked the truncation and the distribution
syntax, so the truncation can't figure out that it's not needed here,
so it'll get calculated. Having said that, it only gets calculated with
real (internally double) values, so there's no hit on memory or on
auto-diff time.
